interviewQuestions.question: How would you detect a draw without scanning the whole board on every move?
interviewQuestions.answerMarkdown:
I'd avoid re-scanning the board for emptiness after every move — that's O(n²) work repeated on every single turn for a check that's almost always "no."

Instead I'd track a **remaining-empty-cells counter** on `Game`, initialized to n² and decremented by one each time `playTurn` successfully places a move. After confirming there's no winner, a draw is just `remainingEmptyCells == 0` — an O(1) check.

I'd also point out the ordering matters: check for a winner *before* checking for a draw, since the board can fill on the same move that wins — you don't want to report a draw on a winning final move.

**Testing:** whether you default to incremental state tracking instead of recomputation, and whether you catch the win-before-draw ordering edge case.
interviewQuestions.subTitle: Detecting a draw efficiently

interviewQuestions.question: How would you add undo/redo to this design?
interviewQuestions.answerMarkdown:
I'd model this as a **move history** rather than mutable in-place edits to the board. `Game` keeps an ordered list of applied moves; `undo()` doesn't try to reverse-mutate cell state directly — it pops the last move and replays every remaining move from a freshly-constructed empty board.

That replay approach is more code per undo call, but it sidesteps a whole class of bugs: partial-state corruption if an undo is interrupted, and keeping win-checker state consistent with a rolled-back board. `redo()` is symmetric — it re-applies a move popped off a separate redo stack, which gets cleared the moment a new move is played after an undo.

I'd note this only works cleanly because moves here have no side effects beyond placing a symbol — a game with more complex state would need each move to carry its own explicit inverse instead of relying on full replay.

**Testing:** whether you reach for replay-from-history over ad hoc state reversal, and whether you can name why full replay is safe here specifically.
interviewQuestions.subTitle: Adding undo/redo

interviewQuestions.question: Why should the set of winning lines be generated once as data rather than hardcoded as separate row, column, and diagonal checks?
interviewQuestions.answerMarkdown:
I'd point out that hardcoded checks ("check all cells in row i," "check all cells in column j," "check the two diagonals") work fine for a 3x3 board but stop generalizing the moment the board size or win condition changes — a 4x4 board needing 4-in-a-row, or Connect-Four-style boards, each need their own hand-written variant of the same logic, multiplying code that's really doing one thing: checking whether all cells in some fixed set share the same symbol.

Instead, I'd generate the full list of winning lines once, at board construction, as plain data — each line just a list of cell coordinates — built by a small generator that walks rows, columns, and diagonals for the given N and K (K-in-a-row on an N x N board), and the actual win-check becomes one generic method: for each line in the precomputed list, check if every cell in it holds the same non-empty symbol.

The payoff is direct: supporting a 4x4x4 board (see the next question) or Connect-Four's shape is a change to the *generator*, producing a different line set — the win-checking code itself, and everything downstream of it, doesn't change at all.

**Testing:** whether you separate 'what counts as a winning line' (data, computed once) from 'how to check a line' (one generic algorithm), instead of writing size-specific logic per board shape.
interviewQuestions.subTitle: Winning lines as generated data

interviewQuestions.question: The interviewer now wants a 4x4x4 3D tic-tac-toe — what in your design has to change, and what stays the same?
interviewQuestions.answerMarkdown:
I'd lead with what doesn't change, since that's the actual test here: `Game.playTurn()`, the win-checker's core loop (iterate precomputed lines, check for a shared symbol), the `Player` abstraction, and the draw-detection counter are all dimension-agnostic already — none of them know or care whether a cell is addressed by (row, col) or (row, col, layer).

What does change is narrowly scoped to two places. First, `Board`'s cell storage and addressing needs a third coordinate — a `Cell(row, col, layer)` instead of `Cell(row, col)` — and however cells are stored (flat array, nested structure) needs to support that indexing. Second, and this is the part that actually takes real thought, the winning-line *generator* needs new logic: 3D tic-tac-toe has far more winning lines than 2D — lines within each 2D layer (same as before, just per-layer), lines running straight through layers (same row/col across all layers), and crucially the 3D diagonals that cut through both position and layer simultaneously, which a 2D-only generator has no way to produce.

I'd close by naming this as validation that the earlier design choice (lines as generated data, not hardcoded checks) actually pays off here: if lines had been hardcoded per-direction in 2D, adding a dimension would mean rewriting the win-check entirely rather than just extending one generator function.

**Testing:** whether you can precisely scope what a dimensional change actually touches, rather than assuming a bigger board means a bigger rewrite.
interviewQuestions.subTitle: Extending to 3D tic-tac-toe
